deep.reconstruction:
Setting (from the previous page). N is highly composite. Write N = exp(θ(p_1)+θ(p_2)+θ(p_3)+...), where p_r is the largest prime whose exponent in N is at least r, so p_1 ≥ p_2 ≥ p_3 ≥ .... Then d(N) = ∏_r (1+1/r)^{π(p_r)}. Replace p_1, p_r by primes q_1, q_r to get N' = N·exp(θ(q_1)+θ(q_r)−θ(p_1)−θ(p_r)). If the sequence is no longer non-increasing, the exponent multiset only gets rearranged, and the rearrangement inequality gives d(N') ≥ d(N)·2^{π(q_1)−π(p_1)}·(1+1/r)^{π(q_r)−π(p_r)}.

The page proves two one-sided bounds and combines them into estimate (1). Together they compare the size of p_r with p_1.

Case A (finished at the top of this page). Take q_1 > p_1, q_r < p_r, with π(q_1) = π(p_1)+n and π(q_r) = π(p_r) − [n log2/log(1+1/r)].
- Then 2^n (1+1/r)^{−[·]} ≥ 1, so d(N') ≥ d(N).
- Since N is highly composite, this forces N' ≥ N, i.e. θ(q_1)−θ(p_1) ≥ θ(p_r)−θ(q_r).
- Use the bounds (π(α)−π(β)) log β ≤ θ(α)−θ(β) ≤ (π(α)−π(β)) log α. This gives n log q_1 ≥ [n log2/log(1+1/r)] log q_r.
- By the lemma log q = log p + O(1) (valid when the π-shift is o(p/log p)), together with [x]/n = x/n + O(1/n) and x = O(r): log p_1/log2 − log p_r/log(1+1/r) ≥ O(r + log p_r/n).
- Choosing n with log p_r = O(nr) (and n = o(p_r/log p_r)) gives the first line of this page: log p_1/log2 − log p_r/log(1+1/r) ≥ O(r).

Case B (this page). Take q_1 < p_1, q_r > p_r, with π(q_1) = π(p_1) − n − 1 (as written) and π(q_r) = π(p_r) + [n log2/log(1+1/r)].
- The intended argument: d(N') ≥ d(N), hence N' ≥ N, hence θ(q_r)−θ(p_r) ≥ θ(p_1)−θ(q_1).
- This gives [n log2/log(1+1/r)] log q_r ≥ (n+1) log q_1, and by the same estimates log p_1/log2 − log p_r/log(1+1/r) ≤ O(r).

Conclusion (1): log p_r / log(1+1/r) = log p_1/log 2 + O(r).

Interpretation (mine). Equivalently log p_r = (log(1+1/r)/log 2)·log p_1 + O(1/r)·O(1). So p_r is p_1^{log(1+1/r)/log 2} up to a bounded factor (≍). Put differently, the exponent r of a prime λ is roughly 1/(λ^{log2/log p_1} − 1). This is the structure theorem for exponents of highly composite numbers.
errors: Case B, as written, does not give d(N') ≥ d(N). With π(q_1) = π(p_1)−n−1 and π(q_r) = π(p_r)+[n log2/log(1+1/r)], the ratio is at least 2^{−(n+1)}(1+1/r)^{[n log2/log(1+1/r)]}. But this quantity is < 1, because (1+1/r)^{[x]} ≤ 2^n < 2^{n+1}. So the step 'proceeding as before' fails literally.

The sign appears to be a slip. With π(q_1) = π(p_1) − n + 1 one gets 2^{−(n−1)}(1+1/r)^{[x]} ≥ 2^{−(n−1)}·2^n/(1+1/r) = 2/(1+1/r) ≥ 1, and the argument goes through. Alternatively, keep −n and use [x]+1 in the second line. The asymptotic conclusion is unaffected.

Implicit side conditions are not stated. n must satisfy both log p_r = O(nr) and n = o(p_r/log p_r), so that the lemma log q = log p + O(1) applies. Hence (1) is meaningful only while p_r is large, roughly for r small compared with log p_1. Uniformity of the O(r) in r is not discussed.
The lemma 'if π(α)=π(β)+x with x=o(β/logβ) then log α = log β + O(1)' is called easy and not proved. It is true: Chebyshev bounds suffice, since π(Cβ)−π(β) ≫ β/log β for some constant C.

results.what: For highly composite N with p_r the largest prime of exponent ≥ r: log p_r/log(1+1/r) = log p_1/log 2 + O(r). Equivalently p_r ≍ p_1^{log(1+1/r)/log 2}, and the exponent of a prime λ is about 1/(λ^{log 2/log p_1} − 1).
results.modern_name: Asymptotic structure of exponents of highly composite numbers (exchange/perturbation argument)
results.usually_credited_to: Ramanujan, 'Highly composite numbers', Proc. London Math. Soc. 1915

results.what: Exchange argument: perturb the θ-representation of N, compare d(N') with d(N), and use maximality of d to get inequalities between θ (hence log) of primes.
results.modern_name: Local optimality / exchange argument for highly composite numbers

results.what: (π(α)−π(β)) log β ≤ θ(α)−θ(β) ≤ (π(α)−π(β)) log α for α > β

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft version, in π/θ notation, of results in Ramanujan's published 1915 memoir on highly composite numbers, where the exponent of λ is shown to be about 1/(λ^{log2/log p_1}−1). Interest lies only in the alternative presentation and a small slip in the second case.

checkable.asserts: The formula d(N)=∏(1+1/r)^{π(p_r)} holds for the HCN 55440 = 2^4·3^2·5·7·11, with p_1=11, p_2=3, p_3=p_4=2.
N = exp(θ(p_1)+θ(p_2)+θ(p_3)+θ(p_4)) for N=55440, since primorial(k) is the product of the first k primes.
With the manuscript's choice −n−1, d(N')/d(N) is bounded below only by a number < 1, so the 'as before' step fails literally.
With the corrected choice π(q_1)=π(p_1)−n+1, d(N') ≥ d(N) holds.
Case A choice gives d(N') ≥ d(N).

transcription_corrections: The transcription matches the image. The second case does read 'π(q_1) = π(p_1) − n − 1' in the manuscript; this is Ramanujan's slip, not a transcription error. The header reads 'Add MS a 94 18 (53)', with circled folio number 53.
